lesson.title: When Molecules Get Real: The Limits of the Ideal Gas Law
lesson.summary: Real gas molecules take up space and attract one another, so at high pressure and low temperature they stop obeying the ideal gas law exactly.
lesson.body:
The ideal gas law, PV = nRT, is built on two convenient simplifications: that gas particles have no volume of their own, and that they never attract or repel each other. Those assumptions work beautifully when molecules are far apart and moving fast, which is exactly the situation at low pressure and high temperature. Under those conditions the space between particles is enormous compared to the particles themselves, and collisions are so brief that intermolecular forces barely have time to act. But push the pressure up or cool the gas down, and both simplifications start to break.

Recall from intermolecular forces that every real molecule, even a nonpolar one, experiences some attraction to its neighbors through London dispersion forces, dipole interactions, or hydrogen bonding. As a gas is compressed, molecules are forced closer together, and these attractions begin to pull them toward each other just as they are about to strike the container wall. The result is that a real gas hits the walls slightly less often and less forcefully than the ideal gas law predicts, so its actual pressure ends up a bit lower than the ideal prediction. At the same time, real molecules are not mathematical points. They have actual volume, and at high density the space available for them to move through is noticeably smaller than the total container volume, because part of that volume is physically occupied by the molecules themselves.

These two effects, attraction and finite size, pull in opposite directions. Attraction tends to make the measured pressure lower than ideal. Molecular volume tends to make the gas resist compression more than a swarm of points could. Which effect wins depends on the conditions, and untangling that competition is the whole point of the Van der Waals equation, covered next.

Consider 1.00 mol of carbon dioxide gas confined to a volume of exactly 1.00 L at 273 K (0 degrees Celsius), a fairly dense, compressed state for CO2. The ideal gas law predicts a pressure of P = nRT/V = (1.00 mol)(0.0821 L atm/mol K)(273 K)/(1.00 L) = 22.41 atm. That number assumes CO2 molecules are volumeless points that ignore each other completely. In reality, CO2 molecules attract each other strongly enough, since they are polarizable and have significant London dispersion forces, that the actual pressure measured under these conditions comes out noticeably lower than 22.41 atm. Exactly how much lower is something we can calculate precisely once we bring in the Van der Waals equation in the next chapter, using this same 1.00 mol, 1.00 L, 273 K CO2 sample as our running example.
